rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Rutherford Scattering Experiment:** Alpha particles were fired at a thin gold foil. Most passed through with little deflection, but a few scattered at large angles (>90°). This disproved the Thomson plum-pudding model and established the nuclear model: a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of the atom's mass.  ·  **Nuclear Size vs Atom Size:** The nucleus is ~10⁻¹⁵ m (1-10 fm) while the atom is ~10⁻¹⁰ m (1 Å). The nucleus occupies ~10⁻¹⁵ of the atomic volume but contains >99.9% of the mass. The rest is empty space where electrons orbit.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Misconception - Mass number $A$ is an integer count of nucleons; exact atomic mass in u is not exactly $A$. The difference is the mass defect, which is small but measurable. Mass spectrometry separates isotopes by their exact masses, not their mass numbers.  ·  Misconception - Packing fraction $f = (M - A)/A$ can be negative because the bound nucleus weighs less than its constituent nucleons. Students expect $M > A$ by adding individual proton and neutron masses, but binding energy release makes $M < Zm_p + Nm_n$.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Fact (Historical): Frederick Soddy proposed the concept of isotopes in 1913, discovering that different radioactive elements could occupy the same position in the periodic table. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1921 for this work.  ·  Fact (Application): Mass spectrometry is used in forensic science to analyze trace evidence, in environmental science to track pollution sources, in pharmacology to verify drug composition, and in astronomy to determine stellar composition.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Atomic mass unit (u):** $1\\\\,\ ext{u} = 1.660539\ imes 10^{-27}\\\\,\ ext{kg}$. Defined as exactly $1/12$ the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom in its ground state. All nuclear masses are expressed in u for convenience.  ·  **Exact mass vs mass number:** The mass number $A$ is the integer count of nucleons. The exact mass in u differs slightly from $A$ due to mass defect. For example, $^{12}\ ext{C}$ has exact mass $12\\\\,\ ext{u}$ by definition, but $^{1}\ ext{H}$ has exact mass $1.007825\\\\,\ ext{u}$, not $1\\\\,\ ext{u}$.  ·  **Isotopes:** atoms of the same element ($Z$ same) with different mass numbers ($A$ different). They have identical chemical properties (same electron configuration) but different nuclear masses, stabilities, and decay modes. Example: $^{35}\ ext{Cl}$ ($75.78\\\\%$) and $^{37}\ ext{Cl}$ ($24.22\\\\%$) are chlorine isotopes.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Nucleus: discovery of nucleus; nuclear density; mass number; atomic number and other topics  ·  **Nuclear Density:** Nearly constant for all nuclei: ρ = mass/volume ≈ A·1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg / (4/3 π (1.2×10⁻¹⁵ A¹ᐟ³)³) ≈ 2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³. This constancy supports the liquid-drop model and the idea that nucleons are closely packed.  ·  Misconception - Isotopes share the same $Z$ but have different $A$; isobars share the same $A$ but have different $Z$; isotones share the same $N$ but have different $A$. These three distinctions are common exam distractors.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Misconception - Standard atomic weight (the periodic table value) is the weighted-average of all naturally occurring isotopic masses, not the mass of any single atom. A single chlorine atom has mass $\\\sim 35\\\, ext{u}$ or $\\\sim 37\\\, ext{u}$, never $35.45\\\, ext{u}$.  ·  Misconception - Binding energy per nucleon $BE/A$ peaks at iron ($A \\\\sim 56$) at $\\\sim 8.8\\\\,\ ext{MeV}$, while uranium has $BE/A \\\\approx 7.6\\\\,\ ext{MeV}$. Fission energy release depends on the difference between parent and daughter nuclei, not a fixed value.  ·  Misconception - $1\\\\,\ ext{u}$ of mass defect is equivalent to $931.5\\\\,\ ext{MeV}$ of energy. This conversion factor is essential for all nuclear binding-energy calculations; omitting it produces results that are off by a factor of $\\\sim 10^8$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Misconception - In $ eta^-$ decay, a neutron converts to a proton, electron, and antineutrino: $n \ ightarrow p + e^- + \ ar{\ u}_e$. The emitted electron originates from the nucleus, not from the orbital electron cloud.  ·  Misconception - Half-life is the time required for a radioactive sample to decay to half its original amount. After $n$ half-lives, the fraction remaining is $(1/2)^n$, not $1/(2n)$.  ·  The nucleus is NOT the same as the atom — the nucleus is the tiny dense central part (protons and neutrons), while the atom includes the orbiting electrons. A nucleus is about 10,000 times smaller in radius than the atom it belongs to.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Nuclear density is NOT the same as atomic density. Atomic density (mass/volume of the entire atom) is about 10³ kg/m³ (like water or solid materials). Nuclear density (mass/volume of just the nucleus) is about 10¹⁷ kg/m³ — unimaginably denser.  ·  Mass number A approximates atomic mass in atomic mass units, but is NOT exactly equal. For example, ¹²C has A = 12 and atomic mass exactly 12 u (by definition), but most nuclei have actual mass slightly less than A due to binding energy (mass defect).  ·  The nuclear radius formula R = R₀A^(1/3) shows that doubling the mass number (e.g., from helium A=4 to beryllium A=8) does NOT double the radius — it increases it by 2^(1/3) ≈ 1.26. This cubic-root scaling confirms the constant density hypothesis.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Atomic number Z determines the element, but ISOTOPES of the same element have the same Z but different A. You cannot tell isotopes apart chemically, but they differ greatly in their nuclear stability (e.g., ¹H is stable; ³H is radioactive with a 12-year half-life).  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Nucleus: discovery of nucleus; nuclear density; mass number; atomic number  ·  Note 4: Remember the units and dimensions involved in Nucleus: discovery of nucleus; nuclear density; mass number; atomic number
